pre.q: Mei has digit cards 4, 0 and 7. She uses each card once to make a 3-digit number. How many different numbers can she make? Write them.
pre.w: 0 cannot be the hundreds digit (047 is not a 3-digit number). Listing in order: 4 starts 2 numbers, 7 starts 2 numbers, 0 starts none. A child who says 6 is using the 3 x 2 x 1 idea without the zero rule.

pre.q: Ali writes “5 hundreds and 13 tens” as 513. Is he right? What number should he write?
pre.a: No. 13 tens is 130, so the number is 500 + 130 = 630.
pre.w: 13 tens is 1 hundred and 3 tens; a box holds only one digit, so ten tens swap for a hundred. Listen for “regroup” or “130”.

invest.title: Mirror numbers
invest.text: A mirror number reads the same forwards and backwards, like 252 or 909. (a) Write 5 mirror numbers of your own. (b) Find ALL the mirror numbers from 200 to 299. How many are there? How do you know you have found them all? (c) Ali says every mirror number is odd. Is he right?
invest.model: (a) Any number whose first and last digits match, such as 101, 454, 777. (b) 10 numbers: 202, 212, 222, 232, 242, 252, 262, 272, 282, 292. The first and last digits must both be 2, and the middle digit can be 0 to 9: 10 choices. A child who lists them by the middle digit in order has not missed any. (c) No: 202 is even. A mirror number is even when its first (and last) digit is even. Extension: there are 90 mirror numbers from 100 to 999 (9 choices for the end digits x 10 for the middle). Look for: the child sees that the end digits match, lists in order, and can say why the list is complete.

pre.q: 4A6 + 237 = 683. Which digit is A? How do you know?
pre.w: Starts at the ones: 6 + 7 = 13, carry 1; tens: A + 3 + 1 = 8, so A = 4. Accept try-and-check if the child then checks by adding.

pre.q: 300 + 150 = 290 + B. What is B? Explain without adding.
pre.a: B = 160. 290 is 10 less than 300, so B must be 10 more than 150.
pre.w: Reads “=” as “is the same as”. A child who adds 450 and subtracts 290 is correct; ask whether there is a quicker way.

invest.title: Odd or even?
invest.text: Ali says: “When I add two odd numbers, I always get an even number.” (a) Test Ali’s idea with 5 pairs of odd 3-digit numbers (for example 345 + 271). (b) Now test odd + even, and even + even. What do you notice? (c) Does the same happen when you take away? Explain WHY, using pairs of counters or a drawing.
invest.model: (a) Ali is right: odd + odd is always even (brute-forced for every pair of 3-digit numbers). (b) Odd + even is always odd; even + even is always even. (c) Taking away behaves the same way: odd − odd is even, odd − even is odd. Why: an odd number is some pairs plus 1 left over, an even number is only pairs. Two odd numbers have two left-overs, and they make one more pair, so no one is left over. Look for: several tests before a claim, then a reason that uses pairs, counters or ones digits, not only “it worked every time”. A ones-digit reason (odd ends in 1, 3, 5, 7, 9) is also fine.

unstuck: tried a digit and checked it

pre.q: A toy shop has cars (4 wheels) and scooters (2 wheels). 6 toys have 16 wheels altogether. How many cars and how many scooters? How do you know?
pre.w: Start with all scooters (12 wheels) and swap one at a time (+2 wheels each swap), or guess and check in a table. Ask “what did you try first?”

pre.q: An array of counters has 4 rows with 5 in each row. A cloth covers 2 whole rows. How many counters can you see? Write a multiplication sentence.
pre.w: Sees that 2 rows are left. They may also say the whole array is 4 × 5 = 20. Listen for “rows” and “in each row”.

invest.title: Where tables meet
invest.text: (a) List the numbers up to 50 that are in BOTH the 2 times table and the 5 times table. What do you notice about them? (b) Now find the numbers up to 50 that are in both the 3 and 5 tables, and in both the 4 and 5 tables. (c) Is every number in the 10 times table in both the 2 and 5 tables? Is every number in both the 2 and 5 tables in the 10 table? Explain.
invest.model: (a) 10, 20, 30, 40, 50: they jump by 10 and are the 10 times table. (b) 3 and 5: 15, 30, 45 (jump by 15). 4 and 5: 20, 40 (jump by 20). (c) Yes to both, brute-forced up to 100: a number in the 10 table is 10 x something = 2 x (5 x something) = 5 x (2 x something). Child-level reason: a number in the 2 table is even and a number in the 5 table ends in 0 or 5, so a number in both ends in 0, which is the 10 table; and every number in the 10 table ends in 0, so it is even and in the 5 table. Look for: organised lists (writing both tables out and circling), the noticing that the jumps are 10, 15, 20, and a test of “always”.

pre.q: A pattern repeats: star, moon, moon, sun, star, moon, moon, sun … What is the 22nd shape? How do you know?
pre.a: A moon. 20 ends a group (5 groups of 4), so 21 is a star and 22 is a moon.
pre.w: Finds the group size 4, then counts in 4s to the end of a group (20) and counts on 2. A child who draws all 22 shapes is correct; ask for a quicker way.

pre.q: Row 1 has 3 cubes, row 2 has 7 cubes, row 3 has 11 cubes. The rows keep growing the same way. How many cubes are in row 6?
pre.w: Finds the rule “add 4” and continues a table. Do not accept 18 (6 x 3) without a reason.

invest.title: Three counting patterns
invest.text: Pattern A: 1, 4, 7, 10 … (add 3 each time).  Pattern B: 2, 5, 8, 11 …  Pattern C: 3, 6, 9, 12 … (a) Write each pattern up to 30. (b) Pick any number from 1 to 30. Which pattern is it in? Can a number be in two patterns? Can a number be in none? (c) Why does this happen? (d) What if the patterns added 4 each time: how many patterns would you need to catch every number?
invest.model: (a) A: 1, 4, 7, 10, 13, 16, 19, 22, 25, 28. B: 2, 5, 8, 11, 14, 17, 20, 23, 26, 29. C: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18, 21, 24, 27, 30. (b) Every number is in exactly ONE pattern (brute-forced for 1 to 99). (c) Counting in 3s, a number is either on the 3s (pattern C), 1 more than a number on the 3s (A), or 2 more (B); there is no other choice. (d) 4 patterns, starting at 1, 2, 3 and 4. Look for: a complete listing, the claim “exactly one” tested on more than one number, and a reason that uses the 3 times table.

pre.q: A machine does ÷ 2, then + 7. The OUT is 12. What was the IN? How do you know?
pre.w: Undoes the LAST step first: − 7, then × 2. A child who divides 12 by 2 first has not yet seen the idea.

pre.q: Mei thinks of a number. She adds 8, then halves it. She gets 9. What was her number?
pre.w: Undoes “halve” with × 2 first, then undoes “add 8” with − 8. A bar or machine drawing is welcome.

invest.title: A magic trick
invest.text: Think of a number. Add 5. Double it. Take away 10. Halve it. (a) Try 5 different starting numbers. What do you notice about your final answer? (b) Is it ALWAYS true? Try a big number and a small number, then say why. (c) Make your own trick that always gives you back the number you started with. Test it on 3 numbers.
invest.model: (a) The final answer is always the number you started with (brute-forced for 1 to 999). (b) Adding 5 then doubling adds 10 and doubles the start; taking away 10 and halving undoes both: (n + 5) x 2 − 10 = n x 2, and half of that is n. A child reason: “double and halve undo each other, and add 5 doubled is 10, which I take away”. (c) Any valid trick, for example: add 3, double, take away 6, halve; or times 4, add 8, divide by 4, take away 2. Check by testing three numbers. Look for: testing small and big numbers, a reason in words, and a trick that really works.

unstuck: tried a number and checked it

pre.q: Ben pays for an 85¢ snack with a $1 coin. Which coins can the cashier give back as change, using the fewest coins?
pre.a: 15¢ change: a 10¢ coin and a 5¢ coin (2 coins).
pre.w: Counts on from 85¢ or takes 85¢ from 100¢. Listen for “15¢”, then the fewest coins.

pre.q: Mei has $5. Three drinks cost $1.60 each. Does she have enough? How much money is left?
pre.a: Yes. The 3 drinks cost $4.80, so she has 20¢ left.
pre.w: Adds $1.60 three times (1.60, 3.20, 4.80). Some children estimate with $2 each (too high): ask if that proves anything.

invest.title: Most coins
invest.text: Use only 5¢, 10¢, 20¢ and 50¢ coins. (a) Pay 35¢ using the fewest coins. How many coins is that? (b) Try the other amounts from 5¢ to 95¢ (in steps of 5¢). Make a table of how many coins each needs. (c) Which amount needs the MOST coins, even when you use the fewest possible? Is there more than one? Why do they need so many?
invest.model: Fewest coins (5¢ to 95¢): 5:1, 10:1, 15:2, 20:1, 25:2, 30:2, 35:3, 40:2, 45:3, 50:1, 55:2, 60:2, 65:3, 70:2, 75:3, 80:3, 85:4, 90:3, 95:4 (brute-forced). (a) 35¢ = 20¢ + 10¢ + 5¢, 3 coins. (c) 85¢ and 95¢ need 4 coins each: 85¢ = 50¢ + 20¢ + 10¢ + 5¢ and 95¢ = 50¢ + 20¢ + 20¢ + 5¢. An amount ending in 5 needs a 5¢ coin, and the rest then needs 3 more coins. Look for: a systematic table, trying biggest coin first, and checking that no smaller number of coins works.

pre.q: Ali has 1/5 of a roti prata. Mei has 1/8 of the same prata. Who has more? How do you know?
pre.a: Ali has more. The same prata cut into fewer parts gives bigger parts.
pre.w: Bigger bottom number means smaller parts when the whole is the same. A drawing of two bars is a good reason. A child who says 1/8 because 8 is bigger is not there yet.

pre.q: Mei ate 3/8 of a pizza and Ali ate 2/8 of it. What fraction of the pizza is left?
pre.w: Counts eighths: the bottom number stays 8. A child who writes 5/16 has added the bottom numbers.

invest.title: Fraction strips
invest.text: Use your fraction strips (halves, thirds, quarters, sixths and eighths). (a) Cover a HALF strip exactly with pieces of ONE kind only. Which kinds work? How many pieces of each? (b) Do the same for a THIRD strip and a QUARTER strip. (c) Can thirds ever cover a half exactly? Why not?
invest.model: (a) Half: 2 quarters, 3 sixths or 4 eighths (not thirds). (b) Third: 2 sixths only. Quarter: 2 eighths only (checked with exact fractions). (c) No: one third is shorter than a half but two thirds is longer, so no number of thirds fits exactly. Look for: children lay the strips side by side and say “fits exactly”. Keep to the strips and drawings: do not teach “equivalent fractions” as a rule (that is P3).

pre.q: A stack has a bottom layer 5 cubes long and 2 cubes deep. On top sits a row of 3 cubes. How many cubes are in the stack?
pre.a: 13 cubes (5 x 2 = 10, and 3 more on top).
pre.w: Counts layer by layer. A child who counts only the cubes they can see is missing hidden cubes.

pre.q: A shape is made of 2 semicircles and 1 quarter circle. If you cut every piece into quarter circles, how many quarter circles do you get?
pre.w: Each semicircle is 2 quarter circles. Listen for “a semicircle is 2 quarters”.

invest.title: Squares joined edge to edge
invest.text: Use square tiles (or coloured squares of paper) and the grid below. Squares must touch along a whole side. A shape that is turned round or flipped over counts as the SAME shape. (a) Find ALL the different shapes you can make with 3 squares. (b) Now find ALL the different shapes you can make with 4 squares. Draw each one on the grid. (c) How do you know you have found them all?
invest.model: (a) 2 shapes: a straight line and an L. (b) 5 shapes: a straight line of 4, a 2 x 2 square, an L, a T and a zigzag (S shape). Brute-forced: 1, 1, 2, 5 shapes for 1, 2, 3, 4 squares (turns and flips count as the same). If a child counts flips as different, they find 7 (L and its mirror, S and its mirror): praise this and explain the rule. (c) Look for a system: start with the straight line, then move one square, and check each new shape against the others by turning the tile.

pre.q: A melon balances 2 apples. One apple balances 3 plums. How many plums balance the melon? How do you know?
pre.a: 6 plums (2 apples, and each apple is 3 plums).
pre.w: Swaps each apple for 3 plums. A drawing of the scale is a good reason.

pre.q: You have a 5 ℓ jug and a 2 ℓ jug and a tap. How can you get exactly 1 ℓ?
pre.a: Fill the 5 ℓ jug. Pour 2 ℓ into the small jug (3 ℓ left). Empty the small jug and pour 2 ℓ again. 1 ℓ is left in the big jug.
pre.w: Checked by a search of all pours: 1 ℓ is possible. Any correct list of pours is fine. A table of pours is a good habit.

invest.title: Weights puzzle
invest.text: You have three different weights. Each weight is 1 g, 2 g, 3 g, 4 g or 5 g. You put some of them on one pan to make a mass. (a) With weights of 1 g, 2 g and 4 g, which masses from 1 g to 7 g can you make? (b) Find ALL the sets of three different weights from 1 g to 5 g that can make every mass from 1 g to 6 g. (c) What do all the good sets have in common?
invest.model: (a) All of them: 1, 2, 1+2 = 3, 4, 1+4 = 5, 2+4 = 6, 1+2+4 = 7. (b) Exactly 2 sets work: 1, 2, 3 (makes 1 to 6) and 1, 2, 4 (makes 1 to 7); brute-forced over all 10 sets. (c) Both contain 1 g and 2 g: only a 1 g weight can make 1 g, and with different weights only a 2 g weight can make 2 g. Look for: a systematic list of the possible sets, checking each mass in order, and the noticing that 1 g is needed.

unstuck: used cubes or coins as weights

pre.q: A box has 9 shapes: triangles (3 sides) and squares (4 sides). There are 31 sides altogether. How many squares? Say how you started: draw it, list it or make a table.
pre.w: Any of the three starts is fine. Ask which one they chose and why.

pre.q: A snail is at the bottom of a 7 m well. Each day it climbs 3 m. Each night it slides back 1 m. On which day does it get out?
pre.a: Day 3. Day 1: up to 3 m, back to 2 m. Day 2: up to 5 m, back to 4 m. Day 3: up to 7 m, and it is out.
pre.w: The trap is 7 ÷ 2 = 3.5 or 7 ÷ 3. A drawing or a table by days shows that the snail is out before it can slide back.

invest.title: Staircase
invest.text: Mei climbs a staircase. She can take 1 step or 2 steps at a time. For 3 steps there are 3 ways: 1+1+1, 1+2 and 2+1. (a) Find ALL the ways for 4 steps. (b) Find ALL the ways for 5 steps. (c) Fill in a table for 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 steps. What pattern do you see? Can you guess the number of ways for 6 steps?
invest.model: Number of ways: 1 step: 1, 2 steps: 2, 3 steps: 3, 4 steps: 5, 5 steps: 8 (brute-forced; 6 steps: 13). 4 steps: 1+1+1+1, 1+1+2, 1+2+1, 2+1+1, 2+2. Pattern: each number is the sum of the two before it (3 + 5 = 8, 5 + 8 = 13). Look for: a list in order (all 1s first, then swap in a 2), a table, and the pattern spotted from the table. Do not name Fibonacci numbers unless a child asks.

common.fast: FAST TRACK. At the start your tutor asks 2 quick questions. If you get both right AND can say why, you may go straight to the THINK HARDER pages and the Open investigation while the group works on this page. You still join the check-together times and talk time. Anyone can move to THINK HARDER when this page is done.
common.preSay: Two quick questions. Write your answer on your whiteboard and be ready to say HOW you know. This is not a test: it helps me plan today.
preDo: Show the Warm-up check slide. Give about one minute for each question. Whiteboards up together, then ask one child per question: “How do you know?” Click to show each answer. Total time: 3 minutes.

Decide quietly. A child who gets BOTH right and can say why is on the fast track: when the worksheet starts (minute 36) they work on the THINK HARDER pages and the Open investigation instead of the core pages, in their own breakout room (or on the main screen with you checking in). A right answer with no reason stays with the group. If you are unsure, keep the child in the group: nothing is lost.

Nobody is labelled. Say “Some of you will start on a different page today; everyone gets a turn at both over the program.” Use private chat to name the page. Children can move at any time: stuck on Think Harder, go back to the core page; core page finished early, go on to Think Harder. Everybody joins the explore, the mini-lesson, the check-together slides and talk time.
common.refSay: One minute, no talking. Tick a face and finish the three sentences on your page: the hardest part, how you got unstuck, and what you will try next time. There are no marks for this and no wrong answers.
common.refDo: Ask one or two children to share ONE sentence (not always the fastest). Never grade or correct it. Praise the strategy, not the speed: say “You drew it when you got stuck, that is what mathematicians do”, not “you were so quick”. Glance at the pages as you stamp journals and use them to plan the next lesson.
